name: Thirteen Days 1962
description: October 1962. Soviet missiles are being assembled in Cuban jungle clearings and a U-2 is about to photograph them. The closest the world ever came — this time, you're at the table.

USA.name: United States
USA.note: Kennedy's America leads the free world with overwhelming nuclear superiority it hopes never to test — and does not yet know what sits in Cuba.

RUS.name: Soviet Union
RUS.note: Khrushchev gambles: missiles in Cuba would fix the strategic balance and shield the revolution — if the deployment stays secret long enough.

CUB.name: Republic of Cuba
CUB.note: Castro, fresh off the Bay of Pigs, has invited Soviet arms and expects an American invasion any season now.

CHN.name: People's Republic of China
CHN.note: Mao scorns Khrushchev's caution as revisionism; on the Himalayan frontier, his armies are ready to teach India a lesson.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.note: Macmillan manages imperial retreat with nuclear weapons and a special relationship, hoping Washington still calls first.

FRA.name: French Republic
FRA.note: De Gaulle, done with Algeria, builds his own bomb and answers to no bloc entirely.

DEU.name: West Germany
DEU.note: Adenauer's republic thrives in the Wirtschaftswunder while the Wall, one year old, cuts through Berlin and the nation. (The map shows Germany whole; the East is under Moscow's shadow.)

EGY.name: United Arab Republic
EGY.note: Nasser, hero of Suez, leads Arab nationalism and the nonaligned between the blocs — while bleeding in Yemen's mountains.

IND.name: Republic of India
IND.note: Nehru preaches nonalignment and quietly ignores the Chinese divisions massing above the McMahon Line.

world.simulationRules: Cold War logic: direct superpower war means mutual annihilation, so conflict flows sideways — proxies, coups, aid, blockades, and brinkmanship measured in DEFCON levels. Crises move in hours, not months: quarantines, back-channels, and public ultimatums. Decolonization churns out new states both blocs court. Intelligence is imperfect — leaders act on photographs, intercepts, and fear. Escalation is easy to start and agonizing to stop.
